content.summary: Welcome to Unit 10. In this reading mission, you will explore texts about different places in town, travel experiences, and talking about future plans using be going to and the present continuous. You will practice reading short descriptions and dialogues to find specific information.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present Perfect with ever and never, be going to for future plans, and present continuous for definite arrangements.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Places in town such as harbour, shopping mall, concert hall, bus station, police station, post office, sports centre, and festival.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific keywords and locations, and skimming paragraphs to grasp general travel plans.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short A2 texts about town places and travel plans.
Locate specific details such as locations, times, and activities in reading passages.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with present perfect ever and never, and future structures.

contextWarmup.prompt: Which place in town do you usually visit on weekends to meet friends or buy things?
options: A shopping mall or sports centre
A police station or post office
contextWarmup.explanation: Shopping malls and sports centres are common places to visit on weekends for recreation and meeting friends.

rules: Use be going to plus the base verb to talk about intentions and future plans, such as I am going to visit the harbour tomorrow.
Use the present continuous tense for fixed arrangements and scheduled plans, as in We are having dinner at the restaurant tonight.
Use ever in questions and never in negative sentences with the present perfect to talk about life experiences without stating an exact time.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Future Intentions and Fixed Arrangements
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up be going to and the present continuous. Remember that be going to is for general intentions, while present continuous is for specific fixed dates and times.
commonTrap.wrong: I am going to meet my friend at two o'clock tomorrow at the cafe.
commonTrap.correct: Use present continuous for confirmed diary arrangements and be going to for general plans.

paragraphs: Tom and his friend Sarah are making big plans for the weekend. On Saturday morning, they are going to meet at the bustling bus station before heading into the city centre. Sarah has never visited the new concert hall before, so Tom wants to show it to her. They also need to drop off a package at the post office near the central town square.

Later in the afternoon, they plan to visit the local sports centre for a quick tennis match. On Sunday, a traditional winter festival is starting by the harbour, featuring music, food stalls, and ice sculptures. Sarah says she has never seen an ice festival in her life, and she is very excited. They are meeting their other friends at the shopping mall on Sunday evening to finish their busy weekend.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Exploring Town and Life Experiences

content.summary: Practical guide on writing about places in town, future plans with be going to, and life experiences using the present perfect tense with ever and never.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Talking About Places and Future Plans
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb + place
blueprintItems.example: I am going to visit the new museum downtown tomorrow.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Expressing Life Experiences with Ever and Never
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have/has + ever/never + past participle + complement
blueprintItems.example: She has never visited the old castle in the city center.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Making Invitations and Giving Arrangements
blueprintItems.formula: Would you like to + base verb + place? / Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing + time
blueprintItems.example: Would you like to go to the cinema tonight? We are meeting at five o'clock.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize proper names of places, streets, and specific locations in town.
mechanicsRules.badExample: we are going to visit central park on saturday.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We are going to visit Central Park on Saturday.
mechanicsRules.why: Names of parks, streets, and cities are proper nouns and require capital letters.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the correct auxiliary verb in the present perfect tense.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He have ever visited the museum.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He has ever visited the museum.
mechanicsRules.why: Third-person singular subjects use 'has', while I, you, we, and they use 'have'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place 'never' between the auxiliary verb and the past participle.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I have visited never the old library.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I have never visited the old library.
mechanicsRules.why: In negative present perfect sentences with 'never', the word 'never' comes immediately after 'have' or 'has'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'never' instead of 'not ever':

practicumQuestions.hint: Replace 'have not ever' with 'have never'.
targetAnswers: They have never visited the old castle.
They have never visited the old castle
practicumQuestions.explanation: The word 'never' already makes the sentence negative, so you do not need 'not'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a short sentence about a place in your town using 'is next to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Where is the post office in your town?
practicumQuestions.hint: Example: The post office is next to the bank.
targetAnswers: The post office is next to the bank.
The cafe is next to the park.

The supermarket is next to the station.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Prepositions of place like 'next to' help describe where buildings are located in town.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Around Town and Life Experiences

content.summary: This module helps you speak clearly about places in town and talk about your life experiences using the present perfect tense with ever and never. You will practice sentence rhythm, word stress in compound nouns, and natural intonation for questions.
content.audioGuidance: Listen closely to the audio models. Focus on linking words together smoothly and raising your voice at the end of yes-no questions.

pillars.name: Compound Noun Stress
pillars.explanation: In compound nouns like shopping mall or police station, place the main stress on the first word to sound natural.

pillars.name: Experience Intonation
pillars.explanation: When asking questions with ever, your voice should rise at the end to show curiosity and engage the listener.

pillars.name: Consonant Linking
pillars.explanation: Link the final consonant of a verb to the starting vowel of the next word, such as visiting a harbour.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The primary stress stays firmly on the first syllable.
Stress the first word strongly when speaking compound town nouns.
Keep your voice higher on the first syllable of concert.
Maintain stress on the first syllable even in plural forms.
